chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Ishaq al-Alawi, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn Suleiman al-Daylami, from Fureyt, from Ibn Abi Yafour, who said:

I was in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when a man from the otter hunters came to him and said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you, what do you say regarding the Salat in the otter (fur)?' So he said, 'There is no problem with the Salat in it.' The man said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you, it is dead, and it is my profession, and I understand it.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'I know it better than you.' The man said, 'It is my profession, and there is none who knows it better than I.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) smiled, then said to him, 'Do you say that it is an animal that comes out of the water, or is caught from the water, and when the water is lost [or it is removed from water], it dies?' The man said, 'You speak the truth, may I be sacrificed for you, this is how it is.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'So you say that it is an animal that walks on four, and it is not like the fish, so its slaughter is its exit from the water?' The man said, 'Yes, by Allah, this is what I say.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Indeed, Allah, Blessed and High, has permitted it and made its slaughter its death, just as He has permitted the fish and made their slaughter their death.'
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray in clothing made from the fur of an otter?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) resolves a juristic nuance regarding the purity of otter fur by distinguishing between aquatic animals and semi-aquatic mammals. He establishes that since the otter is a four-legged beast whose life is bound to water, its ritual slaughter is equated with its death, mirroring the ruling for fish. This highlights the Shia scholarly principle of adapting legal classifications based on biological characteristics rather than rigid categorical boundaries.
